### ¿Se puede conectar con *X*?

No depende de MADRE. Un módulo puede hacer lo que pueda hacer un proceso de Node en tu
computadora: hablar TLS, levantar un servidor, guardar una llave. **Depende de cómo ese servicio
deja que un humano entregue su propia credencial**, y eso cae en tres peldaños:

| | qué pide el servicio | ¿funciona al instalarlo? |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | una llave estática en minutos: token personal, API key, contraseña de aplicación. Sin registrar app, sin revisión | **sí** |
| **B** | que cada usuario registre su propia app (OAuth sin permisos restringidos) | sí, pero el alta deja de ser «pega esto» — y tendrías que escribir OAuth |
| **C** | revisión, evaluación de seguridad o editor verificado | **no**: cada usuario tendría que ser su propio desarrollador |

En **A** está casi todo lo útil: GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Notion (integración interna), Jira,
Slack, Discord, Telegram, Stripe, Shopify, Cloudflare, Odoo, cualquier base de datos, y cualquier
API que acepte un `Authorization: Bearer`. En **B**: Google Calendar y Drive, Microsoft Graph,
Mercado Libre. En **C**: Gmail en lectura, todo Meta, banca.

**La regla**, si no quieres leer la tabla: vale la pena cuando la credencial se consigue en menos
de cinco minutos sin ser desarrollador, se revoca sola, y lo que tu módulo trae o saca cabe en una
línea de la ficha. El catálogo largo y por qué, en
[§6 de `CONECTORES.md`](https://github.com/jossuealcacao-exe/madre/blob/main/docs/CONECTORES.md#6--qu%C3%A9-alcanza-un-m%C3%B3dulo-y-de-qui%C3%A9n-es-el-muro), en el repositorio.

### Un archivo que también es servidor

`toolsForTurn` devuelve `args` que apuntan a un archivo, y tú solo tienes uno. No hacen falta dos:
**el tuyo es la ficha cuando MADRE lo importa y el servidor MCP cuando MADRE lo ejecuta.** Sabe
cuál de las dos cosas es al final del archivo.

```js
import { realpath } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
const SELF = fileURLToPath(import.meta.url);

// …export default { …, toolsForTurn: () => [{ command: process.execPath, args: [SELF], … }] }

const real = async (p) => (p ? realpath(p).catch(() => p) : null);
if ((await real(process.argv[1])) === (await real(SELF))) serve();
```

**Resuelve las dos rutas antes de compararlas.** `process.argv[1] === SELF` parece lo mismo y casi
siempre lo es: cuando MADRE lo lanza, le pasa el mismo `SELF` que ya resolvió el cargador de Node.
Pero en cuanto **corres el archivo tú a mano para probarlo** —`node ~/.pulse/modules/tuyo.mjs`, o
cualquier ruta que pase por `/tmp`, que en macOS es un enlace a `/private/tmp`— `argv[1]` conserva
lo que tecleaste y `SELF` no. La comparación da falso, `serve()` nunca corre, el proceso arranca,
no contesta nada y **sale con éxito**. No imprime un error porque, sobre el papel, no hubo ninguno.
Dos líneas te ahorran esa tarde.

### Si tu módulo habla con un servicio de fuera

Declara a dónde llega. `src/outbound.mjs` no es un registro de salidas: es un contrato, y
parchea `fetch` global para que ningún módulo pueda evitarlo. Un conector que no declara su
destino sale en el registro como «fue a una dirección que nada aquí declara» — verdad, e
inútil para quien intenta distinguir tu módulo de una fuga.

```js
reaches: [{
  id: 'gmail',
  host: 'gmail.googleapis.com',
  to: 'Google · Gmail, con tu cuenta',
  what: 'El asunto y el cuerpo del correo que el agente redactó.',
  when: 'cuando un agente usa la herramienta de envío',
  where: 'MODULES → CORREO',
}]
```

Las cuatro respuestas son las mismas que da MADRE de las suyas, y por la misma razón: quien
lee el registro merece saber qué viaja, cuándo, a dónde y dónde se apaga. Tu declaración se
guarda **aparte** de las del núcleo y marcada con tu `id`, porque quién prometió qué es parte
de la promesa. Se reconstruye en cada carga: desinstalar tu módulo se lleva su destino.

Si apuntas tu módulo a otro servidor en tiempo de ejecución, vuelve a declarar con el **mismo
`id`**: así se reemplaza la entrada en vez de dejar al registro respondiendo por una dirección
que ya no usas.

### Si tu módulo necesita una llave

Decláralas y no las pidas tú. MADRE dibuja un campo de contraseña en el piso `LLAVES` de tu
ficha, acepta el valor **solo desde esta computadora** (`127.0.0.1`), lo guarda en
`~/.pulse/credentials/<tu-id>.json` con permisos `0600` dentro de un directorio `0700`, y anota
en el ledger que se guardó una y **con qué nombre y qué longitud, jamás el valor**.

```js
secrets: [{
  name: 'app-password',
  label: 'APP PASSWORD',
  note: 'No es la contraseña de tu cuenta. Una de aplicación, que puedes revocar sola.',
  where: 'https://myaccount.google.com/apppasswords',   // enlace a dónde sacarla
}]
```

Y la lees por `ctx.vault`, que viene acotado a tu módulo:

```js
await ctx.vault.get('app-password')    // el valor, solo para ti
await ctx.vault.held()                 // [{ module, name, bytes }] — nombres y tamaños, nunca valores
await ctx.vault.keep(name, value)      // guardar
await ctx.vault.forget(name)           // olvidar; sin nombre, todas las tuyas
```

Tu id va cerrado dentro del SDK, así que pedir el secreto de otro módulo no es algo que puedas
*escribir*. La ficha solo muestra que hay una guardada y cuántos caracteres tiene.

**El valor va al entorno del proceso que tú levantas, y a ningún otro sitio.** No al prompt, no
al `brief`, no a un resultado de herramienta, no al ledger.

### Si tu módulo manda algo

Leer se deshace: en el peor caso trajiste algo que no servía. **Mandar no.** Un correo, un
mensaje, un registro en el sistema de alguien más: eso sale con el nombre de quien abrió la sala
y no vuelve.

Por eso el envío vive en `#4` AIRLOCK, donde la regla ya obliga al agente a decir en una línea
qué sale y a dónde antes de que salga. **Lo impone el núcleo, no tu buena voluntad:**

```js
tools: ['buscar_correo', 'mandar_correo'],
sends: ['mandar_correo'],       // por debajo de #4 esta se retira de la lista
```

Si *todas* las herramientas de un servidor mandan, el servidor entero no viaja por debajo de
`#4`. Si alguna no manda, viaja el servidor con la lista recortada y un `brief` que dice por qué
viene corto. Y lo que decides comprobar, compruébalo **en tu servidor y no en el `brief`**: un
prompt es una sugerencia.

**¿Se puede conectar con *X*?** La respuesta no depende de MADRE sino de cómo ese servicio deja
que un humano entregue su propia llave, y está mapeada en tres peldaños —con catálogo— en
[§6 de `CONECTORES.md`](https://github.com/jossuealcacao-exe/madre/blob/main/docs/CONECTORES.md#6--qu%C3%A9-alcanza-un-m%C3%B3dulo-y-de-qui%C3%A9n-es-el-muro), en el repositorio.
Léela antes de escribir nada: ahorra descubrir a la mitad que el servicio exige una revisión
anual de seguridad para dejarte pasar.

El diseño entero de los conectores está en
[`CONECTORES.md`](https://github.com/jossuealcacao-exe/madre/blob/main/docs/CONECTORES.md), en el repositorio. Un conector completo para leer de principio
a fin —CORREO, que manda correo por SMTP sin una sola dependencia— está en
`src/modules/correo.mjs` y se lee en diez minutos. Todavía no aparece en MÓDULOS: lo estamos
terminando, y mientras tanto solo se activa a propósito con `PULSE_LABS=correo`.

## Publicarlo

La ficha de un módulo tuyo trae **GET A NEWER FILE**: MADRE va por el archivo —a la `url` que declaraste o al archivo desde el que lo instalaste—, lo verifica en una copia aparte y solo reemplaza al instalado si carga, respeta las reglas de la casa y dice una versión distinta. Verificar no instala nada.

Y en la cabecera de MODULES hay **+ ADD A MODULE** para instalar el `.mjs` de alguien más. Pasa por la misma puerta que todo lo demás. MADRE lo carga y ejecuta aparte: las API ordinarias pueden leer su archivo y el código del SDK, pero no escribir tus archivos ni abrir procesos. Si ofrece una herramienta MCP, también debe ser ese mismo archivo y corre con esos límites. Cuando Node ofrece `--allow-net`, solo un módulo que declara un destino recibe acceso a la red; en versiones anteriores, el modelo de permisos no restringe la red. La declaración no limita los dominios a los que puede llamar. **El modelo de permisos de Node no es una barrera de seguridad contra código malicioso.** Revisa el código y los destinos antes de instalarlo.

### En el Mercado, para todos

Un módulo tuyo puede estar en el Mercado de MADRE, gratis, con tu nombre. Es curado: el autor de MADRE lee el código, lo firma y lo publica; nada llega al Mercado sin que una persona lo lea.

1. En la ficha de tu módulo, **Enviar al Mercado › Preparar**. Escribe lo que mostrará el Mercado —nombre, una línea y qué hace, en español y en inglés—, el estante, tu nombre y tu usuario de GitHub, y la licencia de tu código.
2. **Revisar** lo comprueba igual que lo comprobará el Mercado: que cargue como carga cualquier módulo, que la entrada diga el mismo id y la misma versión, y qué alcanza su código (comandos, la red, archivos, variables de entorno). Si habla con la red, declara `reaches`.
3. **Preparar los archivos** deja los dos que pide el repositorio, `<id>.module.mjs` y `entrada.json`, en una carpeta propia, y te la muestra.
4. **Abrir GitHub** lleva a la carpeta `modulos/<id>/` del repositorio público `madre-mercado`. Arrastra los dos archivos y pulsa *Propose changes*: GitHub hace la copia y el *pull request* por ti, sin terminal.

En el *pull request* corre la misma revisión y deja el resumen para quien lo lee. Ya firmado, aparece en el Mercado con la etiqueta **Comunidad** y **Desarrollado por** tu nombre; quien lo instala lee antes lo que declara. Para una versión nueva, sube `version` en el módulo y envíalo otra vez.

Desde la terminal, la misma revisión: `npx @jossuealcala/madre check-module --file <id>.module.mjs --entry entrada.json`.

## La ficha

No dibujas nada: declaras, y MADRE arma tu módulo igual que los suyos. En MÓDULOS cada módulo es una tarjeta del tablero y, al tocarla, una ficha con los mismos bloques que AJUSTES. Por eso el tuyo se lee igual que los que trae MADRE.

**La tarjeta del tablero** lleva un ícono, tu `name`, una línea con tu `summary` y su interruptor si es un módulo que se enciende. Un módulo tuyo lleva la etiqueta «Tuyo».

**La ficha**, en este orden:

| Bloque | Qué muestra | De dónde sale |
|---|---|---|
| Qué hace | tu frase, el interruptor «Activo» con lo que dice tu módulo de sí mismo, y la versión con «Buscar una nueva» | `summary`, `status(ctx).status.detail`, `vendor`, `version` o `tracks` |
| Ajustes | una fila por control: su nombre a la izquierda, el selector, interruptor o campo a la derecha; se guarda al cambiarlo | `controls` |
| Llaves | un campo por secreto, lo que hay guardado (nombre y largo, nunca el valor) y la opción de olvidarla | `secrets` |
| Lo que toca | cada cosa que escribe o necesita, con su etiqueta | `creates`, `requires` |
| Comandos | lo que agrega a la caja de texto | `commands` o `slash` |
| Tuyo | traer un archivo más nuevo y quitarlo | el archivo que instalaste, `updates` |

Un módulo que se instala en el proyecto en vez de encenderse conserva su tarjeta de instalación, con el comando a la vista antes de correr nada, dentro del bloque «Qué hace». Las cifras al inicio de la ficha y la ventana propia son de los módulos de MADRE que guardan una lectura (Ash, Intenciones, Ollama); no hace falta declarar nada para ellas.

## El `ctx`

```
ctx = {
  projectRoot, stateRoot,          // el proyecto y ~/.pulse
  config, settings,                // config.json completo y tus ajustes con defaults
  env, agents, room,               // env vacío para módulos tuyos; agentes detectados; sala mediada
  readConfig(), updateConfig(patch),
  record(type, payload),           // escribe un evento en el ledger; tipo "algo.algo", nunca message.* ni agent.*
  language, t(text, vars),         // el idioma de la sala, 'es' o 'en', y tus palabras en él (sdk: 2):
                                   // una frase en inglés que MADRE ya conoce, o la tuya en { es, en }
  services: { history, ollama: { state, generate } }, // lo que el servidor ofrece a módulos tuyos;
                                   // ollama.generate({ system, prompt, json }) contesta con el modelo local (sdk: 2)
  vault: { get, held, keep, forget } // tus secretos, y solo los tuyos
}
```

### El historial del proyecto

`await ctx.services.history({ since, until })` devuelve lo que pasó en el proyecto en ese periodo (fechas ISO; sin ellas, todo). Solo lee, nunca escribe, y lo dicho en `#0` GHOST no aparece:

```
{
  project, since, until,
  requests:  [{ at, chat, to, mode, text }],         // lo que pidió la humana y a quién
  answers:   [{ at, chat, agent, text }],            // las respuestas de cada agente
  changes:   [{ at, chat, agent, mode, files: [{ status, path }], undone }],
  files:     [{ path, status }],                     // lo que cambió y se quedó (sin lo deshecho)
  decisions: [{ at, text, agent }],                  // las decisiones que guardó la memoria
  agents:    { codex: { turns, failed, tokens, costUsd, local } },
  conversations: [{ id, title, requests }],
  totals:    { requests, answers, tokens, costUsd }
}
```

Los textos llegan recortados a 600 caracteres. Es la base de un módulo que informa sobre el trabajo, como el Informe de trabajo del Mercado.

`turn`, en `toolsForTurn`: `{ agent, mode, lease, scratchDir, port, roomDir }`. `mode` va de 0 a 4; en 0 (GHOST) nada se guarda, decide si quieres entregar herramientas ahí.

## Reglas de la casa

- **Nada sale de la máquina por su cuenta.** Si tu módulo habla con un servicio, dilo en `summary` y en `requires`, y hazlo solo cuando el humano lo pida.
- **No guardes credenciales.** Usa las sesiones que ya viven en la máquina.
- **No escribas en el proyecto** desde un módulo; para eso están los modos de los agentes. Un módulo que instala algo en el proyecto es `kind: 'installer'` y muestra el comando antes de correrlo.
- **Falla suave.** Una excepción en `toolsForTurn` entrega nada; en un comando, la tarjeta dice el error. Nunca rompas el turno de un agente.
- **Voz MADRE.** Rótulos en mayúsculas cortos, notas que digan qué no sale de la máquina, `MU/TH/UR › ` cuando hables en un aviso.

## Que lo construya tu IA, en la sala

Escribe `/module <lo que debe hacer>` en el compositor. Es la entrada explícita al flujo guiado: si `#2 CREATE` no está activo, MADRE te pide elegirlo y conserva intacta tu petición. Con `#2` activo, mantiene el agente que elegiste y le entrega el contrato del SDK y el ejemplo. El agente debe escribir **un solo archivo** llamado `<id>.module.mjs` en su carpeta de borrador; no puede instalarlo por su cuenta. Ese archivo trae su `icon`: el agente lo dibuja junto con el resto del módulo y MADRE lo ajusta al mosaico.

MADRE reconoce ese nombre y pone una tarjeta en la sala: `INSTALL FOR EVERY ROOM` o `INSTALL FOR THIS PROJECT`. Léelo, decide, un clic. MADRE lo valida en una copia, lo guarda como `<id>.mjs` en la carpeta que elegiste y aparece en MÓDULOS con la etiqueta «Tuyo». También puedes pedir lo mismo en lenguaje natural mientras estés en `#2` o más; `/module` hace explícito el formato y no concede permisos por sí solo.

Los agentes nunca escriben en `~/.pulse/modules` ni en `.madre/modules`: proponen, tú instalas.

Un módulo tuyo lleva la etiqueta «Tuyo» y se quita desde su ficha con «Quitar» —también desde «Crea tu módulo», en la lista de los tuyos—. MADRE confirma el archivo exacto, borra ese archivo y su registro de origen para actualizaciones, y lo retira de la sala sin reiniciarla. No borra archivos que el módulo haya creado ni sus ajustes guardados. Los módulos que vienen con MADRE no muestran ese botón: no se quitan, se apagan.

## Lo que un módulo no puede tocar

Un módulo tuyo corre en un proceso separado. El modelo de permisos de Node limita las API ordinarias a su archivo y el código del SDK, sin escritura directa ni apertura de otros procesos. Las funciones de `ctx` pasan por MADRE: la bodega solo entrega los secretos de ese módulo y `updateConfig` solo acepta su bloque de ajustes. Una herramienta MCP del módulo usa el mismo archivo y cerco; si el turno tiene carpeta de borrador, puede escribir allí. El modelo de Node no garantiza contener código malicioso: revisa el código y los destinos de red antes de instalarlo. MADRE protege su núcleo así:

- Sus rutas HTTP viven bajo `/api/x/<id>/`; un módulo con rutas fuera de ahí no carga, así ninguno puede suplantar `/api/state`, `/api/messages` o cualquier ruta propia de MADRE.
- No puede usar el `id` de un módulo integrado ni de otro ya cargado.
- `record()` rechaza los tipos de evento reservados (`message.*`, `agent.*`); no puede fabricar turnos ni mensajes.
- No recibe credenciales de nadie; usa, como MADRE, las sesiones que ya viven en la máquina.
- Un error en `toolsForTurn` entrega nada; en un comando, la tarjeta dice el error; al cargar, el tablero avisa cuántos no cargaron y «Crea tu módulo» dice qué archivo y por qué. Nada de eso detiene la sala.

## Probarlo

1. Copia el archivo a `~/.pulse/modules/`.
2. En la sala, MÓDULOS → «Crea tu módulo» → «Recargar módulos». Si el archivo tiene un error, ahí mismo lo dice con la línea exacta.
3. Enciéndelo con su interruptor. Escribe `/tu-comando` en el compositor.
4. Cambia el archivo y vuelve a recargar: no hace falta reiniciar la sala.

Con una IA: pásale este documento y `hello-module.mjs`, describe lo que quieres y pídele un solo archivo `.mjs` con `export default { … }`. Lo demás lo hace MADRE.

# MADRE under the hood

What the README does not need to tell you to use the room, but anyone who wants to understand it, run it under unusual conditions or write a module does. Every claim here corresponds to code in `src/` and has a test in `test/`.

## The ledger

Each project has a stable room under `PULSE_HOME` (by default `~/.pulse/rooms/<sala>/`). Its source of truth is `events.jsonl`: one event per line, increasing sequence, append-only for the room. MADRE rebuilds the conversation window from there even if it restarts or is opened from another IDE.

Writes are serialized across local processes with an on-disk lock, so two IDEs on the same room never produce repeated sequences. The only operation that rewrites the ledger is the privacy purge, under the same lock, atomic (temporary file and rename), preserving sequences.

When the replying agent changes, the room records `handoff.created` with origin, destination and the range of sequences handed over. The transcript remains the durable source; the project is not touched.

An agent's errors are stored, bounded, in `message.failed`: one line of up to 500 characters, without stack traces, and with private terms replaced.

## The stream

`/api/events` is fed from the ledger, not from the process's memory: events that another MADRE process adds to the same room reach the open pages. Polling reads only the new bytes every 500 ms (`PULSE_BROADCAST_INTERVAL_MS`); a file that shrinks, after a purge, resets the offset. Each frame carries `id: <secuencia>`, so a client that reconnects asks from where it left off. A client that stops consuming is disconnected once it accumulates 1 MiB undrained (`PULSE_SSE_MAX_BUFFERED_BYTES`). GHOST events have no sequence: they reach the open pages and never the ledger.

The context window an agent receives is 16,000 characters (`PULSE_CONTEXT_MAX_CHARS`); older messages are omitted before recent ones. A message of more than 20,000 characters (`PULSE_MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS`) is recorded and rejected without invoking the agent.

## The memory

`memory.sqlite` lives next to the ledger and is derived from it: if it is missing or its schema changed, it is rebuilt from `events.jsonl`. It contains:

- `entries` with trigram FTS5: every message, failure and command card outside GHOST, with its sequence. MADRE's canned replies (`synthetic`) are not included.
- `memories` with FTS5: the distilled notes, typed (`decision`, `fact`, `preference`, `question`), with the sequences that support them, who wrote them and their origin (`distilled` or `noted`).
- `entry_vectors` and `memory_vectors`: 768-dimension embeddings, computed in the background and never on a turn's critical path.

**Conversations.** A project has one memory and many conversations. The archive, the crew, the modules and the privacy list belong to the project; a conversation is only the record of one line of work. The first one is the `events.jsonl` that was always there —no file is moved to add this—, the others live in `<sala>/chats/<id>/events.jsonl`, and `<sala>/chats.json` keeps their names and which one is open. Numbering belongs to the project, not to the conversation: opening one starts from the highest sequence any other one reached, so `#1411` means an exchange of this project and the memory index, the citations and NOSTROMO still hold. There are gaps in a ledger and that is fine: sequences are an order, not a count.

Only one conversation at a time drives the crew —two threads editing the same working tree is not a feature, it is a way to lose work—, so opening another one is refused while a turn is running. And one room per project: `<sala>/open.json` holds the pid and port of the server that has it, and another start on the same project is refused with the address of the open room. Without that, two servers writing different conversations of the same project would hand out the same sequence twice and the archive would silently keep only one of them.

**Recall.** When the transcript exceeds the window, each turn also receives, within the same budget (`PULSE_RECALL_SHARE`, 30% by default), the earlier notes and exchanges that match the request. The lexical search weights each term by its rarity in the room: a path or a name weighs more than a common word. With vectors, it is fused with cosine similarity.

**Cascade activation.** Each memory that enters a turn leaves a row with the batch it shared, so the room knows which notes arrive together. From that comes an association —Jaccard over the turns where each one was found by the search itself— and recall keeps two slots for it: when it brings a note, it also brings the one that accompanies it, even if they do not share a single word. Only the turns where the search found them on their own merit vote, never the ones the cascade created, or the network would close in on itself within a few days. The strength is a ratio: a pair that stops co-occurring fades on its own. Threshold 0.34, at least two co-occurrences, and the search never loses a slot to the association. `PULSE_RECALL_CASCADE=0` or the switch in MU/TH/UR turn it off.

**Cold zones.** A memory is cold when three things hold at once: no turn has ever carried it, it shares no topic with any other —so it cannot be reached sideways either— and the archive has been opened at least twelve times since it was written. The third is the one that matters: never-recalled is what every note is on the day it is born; cold is the opportunity that passed it by. Opportunities are counted in turns that actually went into the archive, and only from the day the room started keeping track. NOSTROMO counts them in its header and surrounds them with a faint ring when asked to.

**What to ask.** The room writes the questions whose answer it is missing, always with the words it already has and never inventing a topic nobody raised. Three wells: the questions the archivist recorded as open and nobody answered, the cold memories —asking is the honest alternative to throwing away something that never had its chance— and the kind of note the archive is short on (decisions, preferences, facts; not questions, because an archive short on questions is not fixed by asking for more). They are taken in turns so that a full well is not the whole list, and two ways of asking the same thing count as one. Nothing is sent: the question goes to the composer and the human decides who answers.

**The verdict.** `GET /api/maturity` gathers the six readings, the three tests, the cold zones and the pending questions, and returns a sentence and an instruction. The order is not decided by the score: first what is false (open contradictions), then what the archive cannot answer —and there it points to the questions the room already wrote—, then the weakest reading quoting its own advice, and finally the test nobody has run. Consistency is computed on read; coverage refreshes itself once a day, in the background and only with local embeddings.

**The three tests.** The maturity reading tells what the archive is made of; it does not say whether it works. A test says that, and a test is only worth something if it can fail. `COVERAGE` takes real questions from the history, runs recall at the exact point where each one was asked and compares it with the answer that was actually given. `CONSISTENCY` looks at the contradictions EYECAT still holds, what was taken out of circulation and whether aberrations are being archived more often lately or less. `MATCH` asks the local model again questions that a frontier CLI answered and compares. None of them spends a provider turn; the third runs in the background and can be stopped.

All three are measured **against a control**: inside a room everything talks about the same topics, so to an embedder any pair of texts seems close —the first COVERAGE run scored thirty out of thirty—. To count, what the archive delivered has to beat what it would have delivered for another question, by a margin. Each result says how many cases it had, what it measured with (meaning or words), the bar and the mean against the control.

**Distillation.** Every `PULSE_DISTILL_EVERY` undistilled exchanges, or after `PULSE_DISTILL_IDLE_MS` idle, the archivist reads a batch bounded by `PULSE_DISTILL_MAX_CHARS`, from most recent backward, and writes up to five notes. The archivist is the cheapest allowed one in the order Ollama, Gemini, OpenCode, Codex, Claude; the one that fails sits on the bench for thirty minutes and the next one steps in. A single call per batch, never during a turn. For local models, strict JSON is requested.

**Embeddings.** `PULSE_EMBED_PROVIDER=auto` uses Ollama if it is running with an embeddings model (`nomic-embed-text`), otherwise the Gemini key (`gemini-embedding-001`, the same key the Gemini CLI uses, including the one in the macOS keychain). Batches of up to 100 texts per call. `PULSE_EMBED=0` leaves recall lexical.

**MCP tools.** Each turn attaches to the CLI the `pulse-memory` server with per-run isolated configuration: `memory_search`, `memory_recall`, `memory_notes`, `memory_timeline`, `project_state` and `memory_note`. `memory_note` is signed with the agent and the turn's message, is rejected in GHOST and its notes are marked `noted`.

**NOSTROMO and CODE000.** The server requires the project's designation on `GET /api/memory` and `DELETE /api/memory/:id`. Eight taps on the heart within thirty seconds seal the archive for ten minutes (both routes return 423), eject the console and fire a message encrypted with AES-256-GCM under the room's seal (`<proyecto>/.pulse/mother.env`) that all online agents receive decoded as requester `mother`. If the seal changes or disappears, the room detects it and warns.

**Privacy.** The terms in `config.json` are replaced at four points: the agent's reply before recording it, the index on insert, the notes when saving them and the dataset when exporting it. The purge rewrites ledger, index and notes preserving sequences and the distilled mark. The server rereads the terms before each human message, because `config.json` is shared by all the rooms on the machine.

## The limits sentinel

Each sphere in the bar carries a ring. It shows the provider's real limit when the CLI publishes it, otherwise the local window.

- **Codex** writes in each session rollout (`~/.codex/sessions`) its account windows, 5-hour and weekly, with percentage used and reset time. MADRE reads the most recent one; there is no network involved.
- **Claude Code** publishes `/usage` on Anthropic's OAuth endpoint. With `PULSE_CLAUDE_USAGE=1`, MADRE queries it with the token Claude Code stores in the keychain or in `~/.claude/.credentials.json`; the token only travels to `api.anthropic.com`, as the CLI itself does. It is optional because it involves reading a credential. `PULSE_OFFICIAL_QUOTA=0` disables all provider reads.
- **Gemini and OpenCode** do not publish anything locally: their ring is the local window.

The local window is a soft budget per agent (500,000 tokens) over a rolling 5-hour window; turns drop out of the count as they age, cache reads weigh one tenth and `@madre`'s tokens weigh zero. It warns at 80, 90 and 100% and suggests other agents. A window whose reset time has already passed counts as empty; the monitor rereads the sources every minute and announces `limit.cleared` when a full window goes back to normal.

A quota reader implements `{ id, agent, read() }` and `read()` returns `null` or `{ usedPercent, resetAt, windows?, stale? }`. MADRE never infers the provider's quota from local tokens.

## The adapters

Each agent runs as a process in its own group, with an isolated home that receives only its existing credentials. If it does not respond before the timeout (180 s by default), MADRE terminates the whole tree: SIGTERM and, after a grace period, SIGKILL.

- **Codex**: read-only query; `-C <carpeta> --sandbox workspace-write` in CREATE; in CONTROL, a write sandbox over the project. It generates images with `image_generation` using its ChatGPT account.
- **Claude Code**: local read tools, non-persistent sessions, MCP limited to MADRE's servers. In CREATE, `--allowedTools Write(//<carpeta>/**),Edit(//<carpeta>/**)` under `dontAsk`: the double slash is the absolute form; with a single one, Claude reads the path as relative to the project and denies every write. In CONTROL, writing allowed in the project and denied in the forbidden zones.
- **Gemini CLI**: Plan Mode and an ephemeral read-only policy, extended in CREATE with `allow` rules for `write_file` and `edit` whose `file_path` starts with the folder. It runs with a temporary `GEMINI_CLI_HOME`: OAuth tokens and `~/.gemini/.env` yes; hooks, extensions, MCP servers and memory from the real `~/.gemini` no. Gemini reads `@algo` as a file to include, so MADRE escapes each mention as `\@nombre` and unescapes it in the reply. Under 503 or 429, the CLI retries with backoff for minutes and only writes to stderr: MADRE reads it live, cuts off after `PULSE_GEMINI_IDLE_MS`, retries once with `PULSE_GEMINI_FALLBACK_MODEL` and, if that fails too, says so with the name and the model tried.
- **OpenCode**: ephemeral permissions injected per run, without touching the global configuration; per-pattern `permission.edit` in CREATE and CONTROL. If your configuration does not set a model, `run` picks the default provider, which may not be the one with a session: `PULSE_OPENCODE_MODEL=proveedor/modelo` sets it.
- **@madre**: it is not a CLI. It is a local adapter on top of Ollama that receives the recent transcript, what the memory recalls about the question and the question; never the CLIs' briefing. With an 8,192-token window, because the default 4,096 one truncates the system prompt. What it can resolve without a model, it resolves: identity, orders that are not its to take, requests to save memory and the round table, which is a plan written by the room with one step per online CLI and its wrap-up turn.

The image scopes of Claude, Gemini and OpenCode are fulfilled with **Image Studio**: the MCP server `src/mcp/image-server.mjs`, attached only inside a lease with the scope turned on, which generates with the Gemini images API and saves the file in the turn's folder.

## CREATE under the hood

A turn in `#2` takes the same snapshot as CONTROL, without a seat: several `#2` turns can run at once. When it ends, `diff` against the snapshot: added files are kept and recorded as `artifacts.created` with their path in the project; modified, renamed or deleted ones are restored from the snapshot and announced in `create.reverted`. Forbidden zones are restored the same way as in CONTROL. Each CLI receives its write tools over the project: Claude Code denies `Write` if `Edit` is not allowed on the same path and OpenCode leaves no write tool if `edit` is denied (both verified with the real CLI), so in `#2` they go together and the "add only" guarantee is the restore afterward, not the rule beforehand. Gemini receives only `write_file`. The `scratchDir` under `.pulse/out/` still exists for what has no place and for Image Studio.

In a plan, each step's mode is the minimum of what the orchestrator asked for (`@agente #n:`; without a number, `#1`, or `#2` if there is a lease), the plan's ceiling (the mode of the human message) and the agent's `MAX MODE`. `#4` never reaches a delegate through the ceiling: only with that agent's key. Under a `#3` ceiling, a `#2` step receives a project lease issued in the orchestrator's name and a `#3` step takes CONTROL with its own checkpoint, one at a time. Under a `#1` ceiling, a `#2` step goes through escalation to the human. A `#3` or `#4` step that exceeds the ceiling asks the human for the key for that agent; granting it for the plan does not raise the others' ceiling.

## CONTROL under the hood

Before the turn, MADRE snapshots the project as a real commit under `refs/madre/checkpoints/` with a temporary index (in a project without git, in a shadow repository under the system's temporary directory, with the project as the working tree): it includes untracked files, respects `.gitignore`, does not touch your branch, your index or your stash, and works in repositories with no commits. While the turn lasts, `.env*`, `.pulse/`, `.madre/` and `.claude/settings.local.json` are read-only at the file-system level and get their permissions back when it ends. Afterwards, `git diff` against the checkpoint gives the list of changes; any write into a forbidden zone that got through is reverted from the checkpoint and named. `UNDO` restores the full checkpoint.

## Commands that come back and the copilot

A ```pulse-run stores the mode of the turn that asked for it. When every line that can run has an answer —it finished, or it opened a port and is serving—, `src/room/returns.mjs` builds what the agent reads: why it asked, what it was answering, the end of what it had said and each line's output (head and tail, about 10,000 characters across all of them), and the room opens a human turn marked `auto: 'runs'` with that block, at the mode of the original turn and never above `#3` (`#2` if a line was pressed from the phone). If the agent is still answering or a plan is running, it waits until the room is free; `STOP ALL` holds it until the human hands it back from its card. A request is handed back once. In the shared window, a command's output weighs at most ~1,200 characters: five long outputs no longer push the human's request out.

The copilot is a server window (`/api/copilot`), in memory like the passes: the `#3` key opens it for a time and `STOP ALL` or a restart close it. Each conversation checks it when accepting a message: one in `#3` marked `copilot` does not spend a pass and reaches any agent whose CLI writes. Its turn carries the `copilot` block (`src/room/copilot.mjs`); when it settles, what it deleted is restored from the restore point (`deletesReverted`). Its command requests run on their own when the turn releases the project, only the lines on the safe list, and the hand-back still belongs to the copilot while the window lasts. Eight solo rounds in a row and it stops with an alert.

## Operational recovery

If MADRE stops in the middle of a turn, on startup it detects the `agent.started` events with no close and records a recovered `message.failed` for each one. When closing with Ctrl+C or `SIGTERM`, it interrupts the agent processes in progress, records those turns as failed, delivers the pending events to the open pages and exits. Plans run in sequence and delegates do not delegate. The orchestrator reviews the replies and can open another stretch, up to three per request; `STOPALL` cuts off anything in progress.

## Packaging and tests

`npm test` runs the suite with `PULSE_OLLAMA=0` so as not to touch a real Ollama; no test calls a model. `npm run pack:check` packs, installs into an empty directory and runs the installed CLI: `--help`, `doctor` and a server start that serves the room and closes cleanly with `SIGTERM`. `PULSE_TEST_MODE=1` enables `/api/test/limits` to simulate quota windows.

## GETTING STARTED · THE FIRST FIVE MINUTES

You need Node 22.5 or later and at least one of these CLIs with a signed-in session: **Codex**, **Claude Code**, **Gemini CLI**, **OpenCode**. If **Ollama** is also running with a chat model, the project gets a fifth, local agent.

1. Run `npx @jossuealcala/madre` from any folder: it opens Home, with all your projects and the Coordinator at the top. The first time, a three-step assistant walks you through it: connect the agents (each with its own button to install it and sign in, right there; once for all projects), add the projects (you choose folders inside your user folder; adding does not open them) and open the ones you are going to use. `npx @jossuealcala/madre start` inside a folder still opens that project directly; if there are no agents, the project opens anyway on Connect your agents so you can install them and sign in.
2. The project opens at `http://127.0.0.1:4317`. MADRE opens the browser with its ficha in the address (`?ficha=…`): the browser keeps it and the address is left clean. Pick an agent in the selector or type `@claude …`. The chip next to `to @agente` says which mode the message goes out in; `#1 CHAT ONLY`, read-only, is the default.
3. To add or reconnect an AI later: Settings → Agents (the settings button in the bar, or ⌘, / Ctrl+,), where the agents live alongside the rest of the settings. Codex, Claude Code, Gemini (with your Google account) and OpenCode (with GitHub Copilot) sign in with one click; Gemini and OpenCode also accept their key right there. Under each agent, "Prefer your terminal?" unfolds the same step written as a command, for whoever prefers to do it by hand. MADRE does not store provider credentials: each session and each key goes to its own CLI's file.
4. With Ollama, the Local AI module (Modules, in the bar) is already on: memory is embedded locally and `@madre` appears in the row.
5. Settings → Memory decides who distills the memory and how often. The Memory map, from the Diagnostics header, shows what the project remembers.

```bash
npx @jossuealcala/madre doctor      # which agents exist, who is signed in, whether there is a new version
npx @jossuealcala/madre setup       # the same setup, from the terminal, if you prefer it
npx @jossuealcala/madre start --no-open --project RUTA
```

**On a server, with no screen.** MADRE listens only on `127.0.0.1` of the machine it runs on, and on purpose: whoever reached it could set the agents to work there. Do not open its ports to the network. To use it on a server, open it through an SSH tunnel from your computer. Home uses 4317 and every project you open takes the next free port (4318, 4319…), so the tunnel carries several; if you open more projects, add more `-L`.

```bash
# on your computer: reach the server with the tunnel
ssh -L 4317:127.0.0.1:4317 -L 4318:127.0.0.1:4318 -L 4319:127.0.0.1:4319 -L 4320:127.0.0.1:4320 user@server
# now on the server
npx @jossuealcala/madre --no-open
```

Then open, in your computer's browser, the address MADRE wrote in the server's terminal, the one that ends in `?ficha=…`. The agents are installed on the server and connected from Settings › Agents: Claude gives you a link and a code you paste right there, and Gemini and OpenCode take their key. Use your own user, not root: the agents work with the permissions of whoever runs MADRE.

**The ficha.** Every request to MADRE carries its ficha (Spanish for «token»): a random secret in `~/.pulse/credentials/ficha.json` that only your user can read. The browser gets it once, in the address MADRE opens, and keeps it in a cookie; MADRE's own processes send it in the `x-madre-ficha` header. Without it, MADRE only says that it is MADRE and its version: it lets nobody read your projects, install modules or open #4. Home makes a new one each time it starts and opens the browser; a restart with no browser (an update, a project Home opens) keeps the one before. A tab without the ficha tells you where to open MADRE from. What it does not stop: a program running as your user can read the file, as it reads everything of yours, and the cookie also travels to other ports of `127.0.0.1` you open in the same browser.

**Three names.** **MADRE** is the product. **Diagnostics** is its operational voice: failures, connections, settings. **Log** is the channel the project runs on: the event record, the plan block, the `.pulse/` folder where artifacts land; those identifiers keep their old name, PULSE.

## PERMISSION MODES

Every message goes out with a mode. Your mode is the ceiling of any plan that message starts.

| Mode | Name | What it allows |
|---|---|---|
| `#0` | **INCOGNITO** | Off the record. Nothing is written to the ledger, no one remembers it, it disappears on reload. Tokens do count. |
| `#1` | **CHAT ONLY** | Read the project and coordinate. The default. |
| `#2` | **CREATE** | Add new files and folders where they belong in the project. What already existed does not change: if an agent touches it, MADRE restores it when the turn ends and says so. |
| `#3` | **EDIT** | Edit the real project without per-action approval. One holder per project, a restore point before, a list of changes and `UNDO` after. |
| `#4` | **FULL ACCESS** | Everything in EDIT plus running commands: tests, builds, `git push`, deploys with the CLIs and sessions already on the machine. Files come back with `UNDO`; what leaves the ship does not. The unlock asks for the same key twice: the project name (or your phrase), typed twice. |

**CREATE under the hood.** The agent decides where new things go according to the project's conventions, and creates folders if needed; `.pulse/out/<turno>/` remains as a scratch area for what has no place. MADRE takes a restore point before the turn and, when it ends, keeps what appeared, shows it under the reply as artifacts, and restores any pre-existing file that was modified, renamed or deleted, with a notice in the project. The CLIs receive their write tools over the project and the instruction not to touch what exists; the guarantee comes from MADRE's restore at the end, not from the rule beforehand.

**EDIT under the hood.** Before the turn, a real commit under `refs/madre/checkpoints/` that does not touch your branch, your index or your stash. During the turn, `.git/`, `.pulse/`, `.madre/`, the `.env` files and `.claude/settings.local.json` are read-only at the file-system level and get their permissions back when it ends. Afterwards, the list of added, modified and deleted files, and `UNDO` restores the restore point. Unlocking `#3` asks for the project name; unlocking `#4` asks for it twice. In `#4` each CLI receives its command tool (Codex without a network sandbox, Claude `Bash`, Gemini `run_shell_command`, OpenCode `bash`) and the instruction to say in one line what is going to go out and where before it does.

**Permission request.** If a plan in `#1` reaches a step that wants to create something, the project stops and asks: `GRANT ONCE · GRANT FOR PLAN · DENY`, with a three-minute timer. Only the human grants; a permission written by an agent inside the conversation does not count. A step that asks for `#3` or `#4` also stops: it is unlocked with the key for that mode and that agent. Granting it for the plan does not unlock the other agents.

**A permission with a time limit.** An agent that needs more asks for it in one line with the mode and for how long ("I need #3 for 15 min: …"). Its reply carries a card with the mode, the time it asked for and the options available (#3: 5, 15 or 30 min; #4: 5 min) or just that message; the key opens that window for that agent.

**Copilot.** The robot next to mode · model · effort. It is turned on with the `#3` key, once, for 30 min, 1, 4, 8 or 24 h; `STOP ALL`, turning it off or a restart end it. While it lasts, a message in `#3` does not ask for the key and goes to the agent you are writing to, even if its Max mode is `#2`, as long as its CLI can write. That agent edits the project, builds plans and gives each step up to `#3`, and the commands it asks for that only read —`ls`, `cat`, `rg`, `git status`, `git diff`, `git log`, `node --check`— run on their own and their result goes back to it. Tests, builds, linters and git versions (`npm test`, `npm run build`, `node --test`, `pytest`, `cargo`, `git commit`…) wait for your button, like any other line: they run the project's code, and the copilot may have changed it in its turn (since 1.1.2). What it deletes comes back when the turn ends, it never touches `.git/`, `.pulse/`, `.madre/` or the `.env` files, and `#4` still asks for its own key. After eight rounds of commands without you writing, it stops and lets you know.

**Mode per step.** An orchestrator can ask for each step's mode: `@codex #2: crea la página`, `
…[文件过长——仅保留首 16KB 与末 8KB]…
t stores your things. It does not store provider credentials.
- **What an agent reads travels to its provider.** Codex to OpenAI, Claude Code to Anthropic, Gemini CLI to Google, OpenCode to whatever it is configured with. If `OPENAI_BASE_URL` or `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` changes that destination, MADRE shows only the hostname and blocks the turn before building the briefing; a verified gateway is authorized per agent with `PULSE_ALLOW_CUSTOM_AGENT_ENDPOINTS`. The account, limits and terms of the effective destination apply. `@madre` and the archivist with Ollama do not leave the machine.
- **A daily notice that it is still in use, always on.** Once a day each copy tells madre.run that it is in use: a random identifier the copy created for itself (`~/.pulse/install-id`), the MADRE version, the operating system and the Node major version. Nothing else: no name, no email, no project, no paths, no agents, nothing of what is said in a project; madre.run does not keep the IP. It is how the author knows how many people use MADRE, which versions are running and whether they come back. It goes out through the same record as everything else, so it appears in "What is sent". Without a network, it fails silently. (`src/heartbeat.mjs`)
- **Anonymous diagnostics, on unless you turn them off.** Since 2026-10-28 each copy keeps in `~/.pulse/telemetry/` the failures it meets (the ones Diagnostics knows, with their MU code, and the ones nobody catalogued) and how many turns, modes and features were used. Once a day, and soon after a failure never seen before, it sends them to madre.run with the four facts of the daily notice, its architecture and whether it runs in WSL, then deletes them. - **How each copy runs, its life and whether it is on right now (since 1.1.0, inside the anonymous diagnostics, under the same switch).**
  - **Environment**, as numbers and names of MADRE's own parts:

    - MADRE's language and how it was installed (npx, global, inside a project or from source);

    - whether Ollama is on and how many models it has;

    - how many projects and how many are open;
    - which of MADRE's own modules are on (one the person wrote only counts as «another»);
    - how many days the copy has.
  - **The road to the first message (since 1.1.2):** how many times each step of the welcome was reached, which one was finished and which one was left for later (only the step's name: `welcome.at.project`, `welcome.skip.ai`…); how many projects were created, added, made to try and opened; whether someone who updated with no project was shown the invitation to add one and what they chose (`invite.project.shown`, `picked`, `sample`, `later`); and one count when a project gets its first message. Never the project's name or path, nor what you write.
  - **Life:** installed (a copy that never had an identifier), updated (a newer version opened for the first time, per `~/.pulse/lifecycle.json`), uninstalled (from Settings, sent before anything is removed) and each time Home opens.
  - **Presence:** while MADRE is open, every five minutes it sends `madre.run/api/presence` only the random identifier, the version and the system, so the author knows how many copies are on now; only one of its processes says it. No path, project name, file or anything you write.
  - **It turns off like the diagnostics.** The author's copies send no presence, and madre.run does not count them either. (`src/install-metrics.mjs`)
- **Sends of its own under your switch.** The sentinel, on by default since 1.1.0 (and off if you turn the anonymous diagnostics off), sends redacted reports to the project's collector. The release channel, on by default, asks npm for the latest version: only the package name travels, the same request `npx` makes. `PULSE_UPDATE_CHECK=0` turns it off.
- **Writing.** In `#1` no one writes. In `#2` things are only added: what existed is restored when the turn ends. In `#3` the whole project except the forbidden zones, with a restore point and `UNDO`. In a project without git, MADRE keeps its snapshots in a shadow repository outside the project. A command an agent asks for is run by you, with a restore point before and `UNDO` after.
- **Memory.** Everything said outside INCOGNITO stays in `~/.pulse/rooms/<sala>/` and comes back into the prompts of all the agents in that project. INCOGNITO is the way out for what must not be remembered; PRIVACY, for names that must never appear.

# MADRE SDK · write your own modules

A MADRE module is **one file**. No build, no dependencies, no signing up anywhere. You copy it into a folder, reload the modules from «Create your module» in MODULES, and it shows up on the board with its switch. You can write it by hand or ask an AI for it, with this document as context.

## Where it lives

| Folder | Scope |
|---|---|
| `~/.pulse/modules/*.mjs` | All your rooms |
| `<proyecto>/.madre/modules/*.mjs` | That project only |

No agent can write there: `.madre/` is a forbidden zone in CONTROL and AIRLOCK, and `~/.pulse` is outside every project. A module gets into MADRE only because you put it there.

## The file

The `export default` is a plain object. MADRE wraps it with `defineModule`. There are two complete
examples, and both work as is:

| | what it teaches |
|---|---|
| [`hello-module.mjs`](../sdk/hello-module.mjs) | the minimum: a switch, one setting, a `/hello` command |
| [`connector-module.mjs`](../sdk/connector-module.mjs) | a real connector: key in the vault, declared destination, and **a single file that is the module page when imported and the MCP server when executed** |

Start with the first one. If your module talks to something outside this computer, copy the
second: that shape can't be guessed, and the obvious way to write it fails **silently** (see
"A file that is also a server", below).

```js
export default {
  id: 'hello',            // kebab-case
  name: 'HELLO',
  summary: 'Qué hace, en una frase.',
  settings: { enabled: false, greeting: 'hola' },
  async status(ctx) { return { status: { installed: Boolean(ctx.settings.enabled), detail: ctx.settings.enabled ? 'on' : 'off' } }; },
  slash: [{ name: 'hello', usage: '/hello [name]', summary: 'Saluda.', async execute(ctx, args) { return { ok: true, title: 'HELLO', text: `${ctx.settings.greeting}, ${args[0] ?? 'crew'}` }; } }],
};
```

**Your module does not import packages.** Not MADRE, not the SDK, nothing from npm. Before installing it, MADRE copies your file to a separate temporary folder and loads it in a restricted process. That folder has no `node_modules`: an `import` by package name doesn't resolve and the installation fails. Once installed, each call also runs in a separate process.

**Node builtins can be imported**: `node:fs`, `node:url`, `node:tls`, `node:child_process`. The fence limits what they can do: your module cannot read other files, write directly or start processes. It can use `fetch` or Node protocols for an outside service under the network rules of the installed Node version. There are no packages to install.

If you need `defineModule` —to compute something before defining the module, for example— **MADRE hands it to you**: export a function and you receive it as an argument.

```js
export default ({ defineModule }) => defineModule({
  id: 'mi-modulo',
  name: 'MI MÓDULO',
  // …lo que hayas calculado arriba
});
```

> The modules that ship with MADRE do write `import { defineModule } from './sdk.mjs'`, because they live inside the package. **If you ask an agent to write one for you, it will read those files and copy that line** — and it won't work. Tell it to export a plain object, or the function above.

## What a module can declare

This table is **the complete contract**: 41 fields, not one more. Any other field you write, MADRE
tells you about at install time ("I didn't understand these fields") instead of silently ignoring it. A test in
the suite compares this table against the code, so if they ever drift apart, it's a failure.


| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id`, `name`, `vendor`, `summary`, `creates`, `requires` | Its page in MODULES. `summary` is one sentence: what it does. `creates` and `requires` are short lines, one idea each |
| `version` | Yours, and it starts at `1.0.0`. If you don't declare it, the page shows the file's date |
| `sdk` | The SDK contract your module was written for, a whole number: `1` (up to MADRE 1.0.5) or `2` (`ctx.t`, `ctx.services.ollama.generate`, and a module that is one file importing nothing from MADRE). Without it, it is `1`. A MADRE that does not know your contract does not load it and tells you why; the Market only offers it to the ones that do. The number counts what MADRE hands a module, not MADRE's version: a new MADRE keeps understanding the earlier contracts |
| `tracks` | If your module wraps something from outside, its version isn't yours: it's that thing's. Declare `{ name, npm }` or `{ name, github }` and return the version found in `status(ctx)` as `runs: [{ name, version }]`. MADRE shows that version and looks for a newer one on its own, once a day, with the page's ↻ button to check now |
| `updatePlan(ctx, { latest })` | How that new version is brought to this computer: `{ command, args, display, note, after }`. MADRE shows `display` and runs nothing until the human has read it; the output lands in the room line by line. With no command, return `{ command: null, note, download }` and the page sends you to download it |
| `updates` | An https `{ url }` where you publish **your own module**. With that, its page gets a button that fetches the file, verifies it the same way as an installation, and replaces it if it passes. If you installed it from a file, MADRE remembers which one and you don't need to declare anything: edit it and ask for a new copy |
| `settings` | Default values. They live in `~/.pulse/config.json` under `modules.<idEnCamelCase>`; `enabled` is the switch for every project, and `rooms` keeps what each project said, which wins. MADRE works it out for you: `ctx.settings.enabled` is already this project's |
| `status(ctx)` | What the card shows: `{ status: { installed, detail }, preflight: { ok, problems }, install: { display } }`. `install` is returned from here; it is not a top-level field of the module |
| `status(ctx)` → `runs` | What your module manages that isn't MADRE: `[{ name, version, target }]`. `version` is what you found on this computer (`null` if it isn't there), `target` is what you would install. If it matches `tracks.name`, that is the page's version |
| `toggle(ctx, payload)` | Replaces the default switch; `confirm: 'texto'` asks for confirmation before turning on |
| `onToggle(ctx, enabled)` | Reacts to the switch |
| `ready(ctx)` | What you ask before turning on, in one project or in all (from the Market too): `null` when ready, `{ status, body: { error } }` when not. Turning off never asks it |
| `footer` | Up to two keys beside MADRE's version, bottom right, while your module is on: `[{ icon: 'heart' \| 'star' \| 'link', label, text, action, url }]`. Words can be one sentence or `{ en, es }`; `url` must be https and opens in a new tab. MADRE draws it: on hover it shows `text` and a button with `action` |
| `credit` | Whose idea it was, if it was not yours: a name. MADRE says it on the module's card and in the Market («Idea by …») |
| `icon` | Your module's icon: `{ svg, color }`. `svg` is the drawing — its shapes (`<path d="…"/>`) or a whole `<svg>`, on whatever grid you like — and `color` its tile's, `#rrggbb`. MADRE fits it on its own so it looks like MADRE's: centred and scaled to the same square, drawn in white in one color, on the MADRE color nearest to yours, with anything that is not drawing taken out (scripts, images, links, styles, gradients). Without `icon`, your module wears the grey puzzle piece. Up to 8000 characters |
| `slash` | `/name` commands that run on the server with your `ctx` and return `{ ok, title, text, link }`. The room shows them as a card and the agents read them. `link` is optional: `{ href, label }` with a route of yours (`/api/x/<id>/…`), and the card offers it as a key that opens another tab; an address outside your routes is ignored |
| `toolsForTurn(ctx, turn)` | MCP servers for an agent's turn: `[{ name, command, args, env, tools, sends, brief }]`. For a module of yours, `command` must be Node and the first argument must be **the module's own file**; MADRE starts it with the same permission fence. Another executable is withheld. `turn` carries the agent, mode, lease, folder, port and `turn.turn`: the id of the reply the turn will write |
| `toolsForTurn` → `sends` | Which of your tools **send something outside**. The core withdraws them below `#4` AIRLOCK: the model isn't even told they exist. See below |
| `reaches` | Where your module reaches, in the same four answers MADRE gives about its own. See below |
| `secrets` | The keys you need, declared instead of drawn: `[{ name, label, note, where }]`. MADRE draws the field, keeps it in its vault under your id, and gives it back to you through `ctx.vault`. See below |

| `onEvent(ctx, event)` | Every ledger event of every live conversation in the room, while your module is on. `ctx.room` and `ctx.chat` are that conversation's, and `ctx.record` writes into it. It runs separately: whatever it takes long on or fails at doesn't stop the room. In a module a person installs, each event starts a new process: what you keep in a variable doesn't reach the next one (keep it with `ctx.updateConfig`), and the notices of how much is left of each AI's plan arrive too, even when nobody writes; check `event.type` first and finish quickly. | `controls` | Your module's settings, declared instead of drawn: `[{ key, label, type: 'select' \| 'switch' \| 'text', options, choices, note, invert }]`. In a `select`, `choices: [{ value, label }]` says which phrase the person reads for each value that gets saved (if you give it, `options` comes from there); without it, the person reads the value as is |
| `onSettings(ctx, settings)` | Tells you when the human changed one of your `controls`, in case something live needs to know |
| `conditions` | Entries for the MU/TH/UR catalog, with a remedy per platform |
| `kind` | `'builtin'` (the default) changes how MADRE behaves and lives in `config.json`; `'installer'` writes into the project with a command the human confirms before it runs |
| `configKey` | Your block in `config.json`. By default it is your `id` in camelCase; declare it only if you want a different one |
| `card` | Which card MADRE draws. A module of yours leaves the default value: the named cards are the ones MADRE ships drawn for its own |
| `models` | The models your module chooses between, if it wraps something that has them. They show up on the page |
| `package` | The npm package that installs what your module manages, if there is one |
| `confirm` | A text. If it is there, turning on the switch asks for confirmation and doesn't turn on until the human gives it |
| `toggledEvent`, `toggledBody` | What gets added to the `extension.toggled` event and to the notice the room sees when your module is turned on or off |
| `preflight(ctx)`, `detect(ctx)`, `installCommand(ctx)` | **Legacy**, from when a module could only be an installer. They still work; for something new, return `preflight` from `status(ctx)` as above |
| `describe(ctx)` | MADRE builds it from everything above. **Don't declare it**: it is on the list because the object carries it, not because you have to write it |

### Can it connect to *X*?

That doesn't depend on MADRE. A module can do whatever a Node process can do on your
computer: speak TLS, start a server, store a key. **It depends on how that service
lets a human hand over their own credential**, and that falls into three tiers:

| | what the service asks for | does it work on install? |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | a static key in minutes: personal token, API key, app password. No app to register, no review | **yes** |
| **B** | that each user register their own app (OAuth without restricted permissions) | yes, but signing up stops being "paste this" — and you would have to write OAuth |
| **C** | review, security assessment, or verified publisher | **no**: each user would have to be their own developer |

Almost everything useful is in **A**: GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Notion (internal integration), Jira,
Slack, Discord, Telegram, Stripe, Shopify, Cloudflare, Odoo, any database, and any
API that accepts an `Authorization: Bearer`. In **B**: Google Calendar and Drive, Microsoft Graph,
Mercado Libre. In **C**: Gmail for reading, all of Meta, banking.

**The rule**, if you don't want to read the table: it's worth it when the credential can be obtained in less
than five minutes without being a developer, can be revoked on its own, and what your module brings in or sends out fits in one
line of the page. The long catalog, and why, is in
[§6 of `CONECTORES.md`](https://github.com/jossuealcacao-exe/madre/blob/main/docs/en/CONNECTORS.md#6--qu%C3%A9-alcanza-un-m%C3%B3dulo-y-de-qui%C3%A9n-es-el-muro), in the repository.

### A file that is also a server

`toolsForTurn` returns `args` that point to a file, and you only have one. You don't need two:
**yours is the module page when MADRE imports it and the MCP server when MADRE executes it.** It knows
which of the two it is at the end of the file.

```js
import { realpath } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
const SELF = fileURLToPath(import.meta.url);

// …export default { …, toolsForTurn: () => [{ command: process.execPath, args: [SELF], … }] }

const real = async (p) => (p ? realpath(p).catch(() => p) : null);
if ((await real(process.argv[1])) === (await real(SELF))) serve();
```

**Resolve both paths before comparing them.** `process.argv[1] === SELF` looks the same and almost
always is: when MADRE launches it, it passes the same `SELF` that Node's loader already resolved.
But as soon as **you run the file yourself by hand to test it** —`node ~/.pulse/modules/tuyo.mjs`, or
any path that goes through `/tmp`, which on macOS is a link to `/private/tmp`— `argv[1]` keeps
what you typed and `SELF` doesn't. The comparison comes out false, `serve()` never runs, the process starts,
answers nothing and **exits successfully**. It doesn't print an error because, on paper, there wasn't one.
Two lines save you that afternoon.

### If your module talks to an outside service

Declare where it reaches. `src/outbound.mjs` is not a log of outgoing traffic: it is a contract, and
it patches global `fetch` so that no module can get around it. A connector that doesn't declare its
destination shows up in the log as "went to an address nothing here declares" — true, and
useless to someone trying to tell your module apart from a leak.

```js
reaches: [{
  id: 'gmail',
  host: 'gmail.googleapis.com',
  to: 'Google · Gmail, con tu cuenta',
  what: 'El asunto y el cuerpo del correo que el agente redactó.',
  when: 'cuando un agente usa la herramienta de envío',
  where: 'MODULES → CORREO',
}]
```

The four answers are the same ones MADRE gives about its own, and for the same reason: whoever
reads the log deserves to know what travels, when, where to, and where it's turned off. Your declaration is
stored **separately** from the core's and marked with your `id`, because who promised what is part
of the promise. It is rebuilt on every load: uninstalling your module takes its destination with it.

If you point your module at another server at runtime, declare again with the **same
`id`**: that way the entry is replaced instead of leaving the log answering for an address
you no longer use.

### If your module needs a key

Declare them and don't ask for them yourself. MADRE draws a password field on the `KEYS` floor of your
page, accepts the value **only from this computer** (`127.0.0.1`), stores it in
`~/.pulse/credentials/<tu-id>.json` with `0600` permissions inside a `0700` directory, and notes
in the ledger that one was saved and **with what name and what length, never the value**.

```js
secrets: [{
  name: 'app-password',
  label: 'APP PASSWORD',
  note: 'No es la contraseña de tu cuenta. Una de aplicación, que puedes revocar sola.',
  where: 'https://myaccount.google.com/apppasswords',   // enlace a dónde sacarla
}]
```

And you read it through `ctx.vault`, which comes scoped to your module:

```js
await ctx.vault.get('app-password')    // el valor, solo para ti
await ctx.vault.held()                 // [{ module, name, bytes }] — nombres y tamaños, nunca valores
await ctx.vault.keep(name, value)      // guardar
await ctx.vault.forget(name)           // olvidar; sin nombre, todas las tuyas
```

Your id is sealed inside the SDK, so asking for another module's secret is not something you can
*write*. The page only shows that one is stored and how many characters it has.

**The value goes to the environment of the process you start, and nowhere else.** Not to the prompt, not
to the `brief`, not to a tool result, not to the ledger.

### If your module sends something

Reading can be undone: in the worst case you brought in something that wasn't useful. **Sending can't.** An email, a
message, a record in someone else's system: that goes out under the name of whoever opened the room
and doesn't come back.

That's why sending lives in `#4` AIRLOCK, where the rule already requires the agent to say in one line
what goes out and where before it goes out. **The core enforces it, not your good will:**

```js
tools: ['buscar_correo', 'mandar_correo'],
sends: ['mandar_correo'],       // por debajo de #4 esta se retira de la lista
```

If *all* of a server's tools send, the whole server doesn't travel below
`#4`. If some don't send, the server travels with the list trimmed and a `brief` that says why
it comes short. And whatever you decide to check, check it **in your server and not in the `brief`**: a
prompt is a suggestion.

**Can it connect to *X*?** The answer doesn't depend on MADRE but on how that service lets
a human hand over their own key, and it is mapped in three tiers —with a catalog— in
[§6 of `CONECTORES.md`](https://github.com/jossuealcacao-exe/madre/blob/main/docs/en/CONNECTORS.md#6--qu%C3%A9-alcanza-un-m%C3%B3dulo-y-de-qui%C3%A9n-es-el-muro), in the repository.
Read it before writing anything: it saves you discovering halfway through that the service requires an annual
security review to let you in.

The whole design of the connectors is in
[`CONECTORES.md`](https://github.com/jossuealcacao-exe/madre/blob/main/docs/en/CONNECTORS.md), in the repository. A complete connector to read from beginning
to end —CORREO, which sends email over SMTP without a single dependency— is in
`src/modules/correo.mjs` and takes ten minutes to read. It doesn't appear in MODULES yet: we're
finishing it, and in the meantime it can only be turned on deliberately with `PULSE_LABS=correo`.

## Publishing it

The page of a module of yours has **GET A NEWER FILE**: MADRE fetches the file —from the `url` you declared or from the file you installed it from—, verifies it in a separate copy, and only replaces the installed one if it loads, follows the house rules, and states a different version. Verifying installs nothing.

And in the MODULES header there is **+ ADD A MODULE** to install someone else's `.mjs`. It goes through the same door as everything else. MADRE loads and runs it separately: ordinary APIs can read the module file and SDK code, but cannot directly write your files or start processes. An MCP tool it offers must use that same file and limits. Where Node offers `--allow-net`, only modules declaring an outside destination receive network access; older versions do not restrict network access. A declaration does not limit the hosts it can contact. **Node's permission model is not a security boundary against malicious code.** Review the code and destinations before installing it.

### In the Market, for everyone

A module of yours can be in MADRE's Market, free, with your name on it. It is curated: the author of MADRE reads the code, signs it and publishes it; nothing reaches the Market without a person reading it.

1. On your module's page, **Send to the Market › Prepare**. Write what the Market will show —name, one line and what it does, in Spanish and English—, the shelf, your name and GitHub user, and the license of your code.
2. **Check** checks it the way the Market will: that it loads as any module loads, that the entry says the same id and version, and what its code reaches for (commands, the network, files, environment variables). If it talks to the network, declare `reaches`.
3. **Prepare the files** leaves the two the repository asks for, `<id>.module.mjs` and `entrada.json`, in a folder of their own, and shows it to you.
4. **Open GitHub** takes you to the `modulos/<id>/` folder of the public `madre-mercado` repository. Drag both files in and press *Propose changes*: GitHub makes the fork and the pull request for you, no terminal.

The same check runs on the pull request and leaves its summary for whoever reads it. Once signed, it shows in the Market tagged **Community** and **Developed by** your name; whoever installs it reads what it declares first. For a new version, raise `version` in the module and send it again.

From the terminal, the same check: `npx @jossuealcala/madre check-module --file <id>.module.mjs --entry entrada.json`.

## The module page

You don't draw anything: you declare, and MADRE builds your module the same way as its own. In MODULES each module is a card on the board and, when you tap it, a page with the same blocks as SETTINGS. That's why yours reads the same as the ones MADRE ships.

**The board card** has an icon, your `name`, a line with your `summary`, and its switch if it is a module that gets turned on. A module of yours carries the «Yours» tag.

**The page**, in this order:

| Block | What it shows | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| What it does | your sentence, the «Active» switch with what your module says about itself, and the version with «Look for a newer one» | `summary`, `status(ctx).status.detail`, `vendor`, `version` or `tracks` |
| Settings | one row per control: its name on the left, the selector, switch, or field on the right; it saves when you change it | `controls` |
| Keys | one field per secret, what is stored (name and length, never the value), and the option to forget it | `secrets` |
| What it touches | each thing it writes or needs, with its label | `creates`, `requires` |
| Commands | what it adds to the text box | `commands` or `slash` |
| Yours | get a newer file and remove it | the file you installed, `updates` |

A module that installs into the project instead of being turned on keeps its install card, with the command in view before anything runs, inside the «What it does» block. The figures at the top of the page and the dedicated window belong to MADRE's modules that keep a reading (Ash, Suggested effort, Ollama); you don't need to declare anything for them.

## The `ctx`

```
ctx = {
  projectRoot, stateRoot,          // el proyecto y ~/.pulse
  config, settings,                // config.json completo y tus ajustes con defaults
  env, agents, room,               // empty env for your modules; detected agents; mediated room
  readConfig(), updateConfig(patch),
  record(type, payload),           // escribe un evento en el ledger; tipo "algo.algo", nunca message.* ni agent.*
  language, t(text, vars),         // the room's language, 'es' or 'en', and your words in it (sdk: 2):
                                   // an English sentence MADRE already knows, or your own { es, en }
  services: { history, ollama: { state, generate } }, // what the server offers your modules;
                                   // ollama.generate({ system, prompt, json }) answers with the local model (sdk: 2)

```

### The project's history

`await ctx.services.history({ since, until })` returns what happened in the project in that period (ISO dates; without them, all of it). It only reads, never writes, and what was said in `#0` GHOST is not there:

```
{
  project, since, until,
  requests:  [{ at, chat, to, mode, text }],         // what the human asked, and of whom
  answers:   [{ at, chat, agent, text }],            // each agent's answers
  changes:   [{ at, chat, agent, mode, files: [{ status, path }], undone }],
  files:     [{ path, status }],                     // what changed and stayed (without what was undone)
  decisions: [{ at, text, agent }],                  // the decisions the memory kept
  agents:    { codex: { turns, failed, tokens, costUsd, local } },
  conversations: [{ id, title, requests }],
  totals:    { requests, answers, tokens, costUsd }
}
```

Texts come cut at 600 characters. It is the ground for a module that reports on the work, like the Market's Work report.

`turn`, in `toolsForTurn`: `{ agent, mode, lease, scratchDir, port, roomDir }`. `mode` goes from 0 to 4; in 0 (GHOST) nothing is saved, so decide whether you want to hand over tools there.

## House rules

- **Nothing leaves the machine on its own.** If your module talks to a service, say so in `summary` and in `requires`, and do it only when the human asks for it.
- **Don't store credentials.** Use the sessions that already live on the machine.
- **Don't write into the project** from a module; that's what the agents' modes are for. A module that installs something into the project is `kind: 'installer'` and shows the command before running it.
- **Fail softly.** An exception in `toolsForTurn` hands over nothing; in a command, the card states the error. Never break an agent's turn.
- **MADRE's voice.** Short uppercase labels, notes that say what doesn't leave the machine, `MU/TH/UR › ` when you speak in a notice.

## Let your AI build it, in the room

Type `/module <lo que debe hacer>` in the composer. It is the explicit entry point to the guided flow: if `#2 CREATE` isn't active, MADRE asks you to choose it and keeps your request intact. With `#2` active, it keeps the agent you chose and hands it the SDK contract and the example. The agent must write **a single file** named `<id>.module.mjs` in its scratch folder; it cannot install it on its own. That file carries its `icon`: the agent draws it with the rest of the module and MADRE fits it to the tile.

MADRE recognizes that name and puts a card in the room: `INSTALL FOR EVERY ROOM` or `INSTALL FOR THIS PROJECT`. Read it, decide, one click. MADRE validates it in a copy, saves it as `<id>.mjs` in the folder you chose, and it appears in MODULES with the «Yours» tag. You can also ask for the same thing in natural language while you're in `#2` or higher; `/module` makes the format explicit and doesn't grant permissions on its own.

Agents never write to `~/.pulse/modules` or `.madre/modules`: they propose, you install.

A module of yours carries the «Yours» tag and is removed from its page with «Remove» —also from «Create your module», in the list of yours—. MADRE confirms the exact file, deletes that file and its origin record for updates, and withdraws it from the room without restarting it. It doesn't delete files the module created or its saved settings. The modules that ship with MADRE don't show that button: they aren't removed, they're turned off.

## What a module cannot touch

A module of yours runs in a separate process. Node limits ordinary APIs to its file and the SDK code and denies direct writes and child processes. The `ctx` functions pass through MADRE: the vault returns only that module's secrets, and `updateConfig` accepts only its settings block. Its one-file MCP server uses the same limits and may write to the turn's scratch folder when one exists. Node does not guarantee containment of malicious code: review its code and network destinations before installing it. MADRE also protects its core like this:

- Its HTTP routes live under `/api/x/<id>/`; a module with routes outside that doesn't load, so none can impersonate `/api/state`, `/api/messages`, or any route of MADRE's own.
- It cannot use the `id` of a built-in module or of another one already loaded.
- `record()` rejects the reserved event types (`message.*`, `agent.*`); it cannot fabricate turns or messages.
- It receives nobody's credentials; like MADRE, it uses the sessions that already live on the machine.
- An error in `toolsForTurn` hands over nothing; in a command, the card states the error; at load time, the board warns how many didn't load and «Create your module» says which file and why. None of that stops the room.

## Testing it

1. Copy the file to `~/.pulse/modules/`.
2. In the room, MODULES → «Create your module» → «Reload modules». If the file has an error, it tells you right there with the exact line.
3. Turn it on with its switch. Type `/tu-comando` in the composer.
4. Change the file and reload again: no need to restart the room.

With an AI: give it this document and `hello-module.mjs`, describe what you want, and ask it for a single `.mjs` file with `export default { … }`. MADRE does the rest.
